    1      Introduction
Let G be an n-vertex weighted graph. A spanner of G is a subgraph that approximately
preserves distances. Formally, a subgraph H is a t-spanner of G if distH (u, v) ≤ t · distG (u, v)
for all u, v ∈ V (where distX denotes the shortest path distance in a graph X). Since their
introduction by Peleg and Ullman [26] and Peleg and Schäffer [24], spanners have been
found to be extremely useful for a wide variety of applications, including network tasks like
routing and synchronization [25, 29, 13, 14, 26], preconditioning linear systems [17], distance
estimation [30, 7], and many others.
    The first tight construction, and one of the most influential spanner constructions, was
given by [5], which described a simple greedy algorithm that produces a (2k − 1)-spanner of
a graph G, of size O(n1+ k ) edges, which is best possible1 .
                            1


    To bypass this size-stretch tradeoff, much work has gone into finding better ways to
parameterize how shortest paths in G may stretch in H. The most well-studied such
generalization is (α, β)-spanners which allow a multiplicative stretch α (which may be viewed
as the effective stretch for pairs that are sufficiently far apart in the graph), plus an additive
stretch β which is used to mask the local barrier of the stretch of the endpoints of an edge in
a high girth graph. Let Wmax (G) denote the maximum weight of an edge in G.

▶ Definition 1 ((α, β)-spanner). A subgraph H ⊆ G is an (α, β)-spanner of G if for every
u, v ∈ V ,

        distH (u, v) ≤ α · distG (u, v) + β · Wmax (G).

       The quest to handle weights
       Spanners are often used to compress metric spaces that correspond to weighted input graphs,
       see e.g. [10, 15, 22, 28]. While standard multiplicative spanners can handle weights easily,
       algorithms that construct (α, β)-spanners for unweighted graphs typically take non-trivial
       effort to be adapted to handle weights. A notable example is the +6 spanner [6, 20], where
       extending the construction to weighted graphs required three separate works [4, 19, 21].
       Initially, the work of Cohen [12] constructed weighted (1 + ε, β) spanners, which was then
       improved by [16]. In recent years, there has been a renewed and growing interest in
       understanding spanners for weighted graphs. The work of [18] achieved constructions of
       weighted (α, β) spanners with local stretch, meaning that Wmax (G) is replaced by Wmax (P ),
       which stands for the smallest maximum edge weight along a shortest path P between nodes.
       A sequence of recent works [4, 19, 2, 21] gave tight bounds for weighted additive spanners. A
       key ingredient in these works is the work of Knudsen [20], which describes a simple algorithm
       to obtain additive spanners greedily.

       Handling weights: beyond additive stretch

       The “local” recipe for (α, β) spanners, and how it fails to handle weights
       We now explain why existing constructions of (α, β)-spanners fail to handle weighted graphs,
       e.g. those of [6, 9, 11, 27]. When the graph G is unweighted, obtaining an (α, β) spanner can
       be done “locally” by guaranteeing good stretch for paths of fixed length. For example, to
       obtain a (k, k − 1)-spanner for an unweighted graph G, one can take a standard spanner H1
       that guarantees a stretch of 2k − 1 for a single edge, and a subgraph H2 which guarantees
       a stretch of k for vertices of distance 2. H1 ∪ H2 is the desired spanner - indeed given x, y
       with a shortest path P := Px,y with t edges in G, break P into ⌊t/2⌋ paths of length 2
       with an extra edge remaining if t is odd, and use H2 to replace the length 2 paths, and
       H1 to replace the remaining single edge. As it turns out, such a “recipe” cannot yield a
       (k, k − 1)-spanner for weighted graphs. In a recent work, Popova and Tzalik [27] proved that
       in any weighted graph G the best approximation one can provide for a path P of length 2 is
       Wmin (P ) + (2k − 1)Wmax (P )3 , assuming the desired size bound on the spanner is O(n1+1/k ),
       hence in particular, such an approach may incur an additive +(2k − 2)Wmax (G) error on
       every second edge along the path, whereas a (k, k − 1)-spanner allows a (k − 1)Wmax (G)
       additive error only once along the path.
           Putting it all together, recent works have investigated how to construct weighted (α, β)-
       spanners, and while the important case of additive spanners (α = 1) has been resolved
       in [4, 19, 2, 21], the general case of α > 1 has resisted progress, with only a single known

    The (k, k − 1)-spanners we construct can be viewed as a spanner whose multiplicative
stretch is roughly half the multiplicative stretch of the classical greedy spanner, while still
allowing for a single bottleneck, reflected in the additive (k − 1) term. To our knowledge,
prior to this work there was no known construction of an (α, β) spanner that improves upon
the stretch of the greedy algorithm for weighted graphs, and with similar size.5


Conceptual contribution
Beyond the (k, k − 1) construction, the main contribution of this work is a new global greedy
completion paradigm for constructing weighted (α, β)-spanners. The algorithm extends
Knudsen’s additive completion by introducing a notion of minimal segmentations of shortest
paths, and repairing only the bottlenecks that violate the target stretch. This avoids the
over-correction inherent in naive greedy approaches, and crucially enables handling weighted
graphs, where local path-based constructions fail. Interestingly, the analysis gives insight
towards the actual structure of the replacement shortest paths, beyond just the (α, β) stretch
guarantee, and leads to interesting new direction, described in Section 5.


Comparison to [27]
The two works study different aspects of greedy spanner constructions. The focus of [27] is
on greedy constructions of d → r spanners in unweighted graphs, namely subgraphs in which
every pair of vertices at distance exactly d in G has distance at most r in the spanner. Such
constructions naturally serve as local ingredients in the design of unweighted (α, β)-spanners,
and their analysis relies on clustering, ball-growth, and path-buying arguments around
short paths. In contrast, the present work studies weighted (α, β)-spanners directly. As
explained previously, the more challenging weighted setting, is inherently global and requires
new methods. Consequently, both the algorithm and the analysis in the present paper are
completely different.

           2      Technical Overview
       Throughout the technical overview we assume for simplicity the graph G is unweighted. The
       fact that the proposed algorithm is global, in the sense that it is independent of the actual
       number of edges along a path, makes it possible to handle weighted graphs.

       2.1        Knudsen’s algorithm
       Knudsen’s algorithm takes as input a graph G, and an integer β, and produces a +β spanner
       of G. It consists of 2 main phases:
          (Initialize) Compute an initial graph H0 , obtained by going over all v ∈ V and adding nγ
          arbitrary neighboring edges to v. Set H ← H0 .
          (Additive Completion) While there exist x, y such that distH (x, y) > distG (x, y) + β: Find
          an x-to-y shortest path Px,y . Add to H all edges of Px,y missing from H.

           We now give a high-level overview of the analysis. The analysis hinges on showing that
       in each completion step, if in the ith step ti new edges along Px,y are added, then Ω(ti n1−γ )
       pairs6 of vertices have their distance substantially improved by the completion step, meaning
       that if H is the graph before the completion step, and H ′ is the graph after the completion
       step, then for Ω(ti n1−γ ) pairs (u, v) we have distH (u, v) − distH ′ (u, v) ≥ 1. Moreover, in the
       first H for which (u, v) improves, we have distH ′ (u, v) ≤ distG (u, v) + O(1). Combining the
       fact that a pair (u, v) is within O(1) of its distance in G, after the first improvement, there
       can be O(1) additional steps for which distH (u, v) − distH ′ (u, v) ≥ 1. Therefore one gets
       that i Ω(ti n1−γ ) = O(n2 ), hence i ti = O(n1+γ ). In conclusion the final size bound of

       2.2        Defining the (α, β)-completion
       As usual with greedy algorithms, correctness is straightforward; the main challenge is to
       show that the final output is sparse. We now describe the main conceptual contribution
       of the paper, which lies in finding the right way to define the (α, β)-completion in a way
       that preserves correctness and, crucially, allows one to prove a good bound on the size of the
       output graph. To do so, we incorporate two delicate adaptations to Knudsen’s algorithm.
       We describe the algorithm progressively, through a sequence of increasingly refined attempts.
       Assume we are given a graph G, parameters (α, β), and some initial graph H0 to be completed
       to an (α, β)-spanner of G. A natural first attempt is to apply Knudsen’s original idea directly.

       Attempt 1 (unsuccessful): naive (α, β)-completion
       While there exist x, y such that:

               distH (x, y) > α · distG (x, y) + β.

       Find an x-to-y shortest path Px,y . Add to H all edges of Px,y missing from H.

    The naive (α, β)-completion successfully fixes pairs x, y with bad stretch – but at what
cost? The key problem with the naive completion is its over-correction. If initially x, y
satisfied distH (x, y) = α · distG (x, y) + β + 1, it seems plausible that a small fix could have
done the job. On the other hand, by adding all missing edges along Px,y we make the distance
between x, y in the new graph equal to their actual distance in G - this indeed fixes the bad
stretch of x, y, but it seems to take it too far.

Attempt 2 (unsuccessful): (α, β)-completion by fixing the bottlenecks
The key observation is that we can find a mild fix to the distance of x, y by only fixing the
bottlenecks along a shortest path. Let Px,y be an x-to-y shortest path, and let e be an edge
on Px,y . Say e = {u, v} has α-distant endpoints in H if distH (u, v) > α · distG (u, v). The
key observation is that if all α-distant edges are added along the path, then in the new
graph H ′ distH ′ (x, y) ≤ α · distG (x, y), hence this still fixes the pair x, y, but now only the
“bottlenecks” along the path are added to H, which helps ensure that only a few edges are
added.
   Formally the new (α, β)-completion is:
While there exist x, y such that:

    distH (x, y) > α · distG (x, y) + β.

Find an x-to-y shortest path Px,y . Add to H all the α-distant edges of Px,y missing from H.
   This idea is close to the final algorithm, but one additional ingredient is needed to control
the total number of added edges.

Attempt 3 (successful): incorporating shortcuts
The last optimization is to allow bypassing bottlenecks along Px,y if possible. The key
observation is that it may be the case that for example e1 = (u, v), e2 = (v, w), e3 = (w, x)
are three consecutive edges along Px,y which are all α-distant, yet distH (u, x) ≤ α·distG (u, x).
Hence if we can find in H a path of stretch α between endpoints of α-distant edges which we
can use to “jump over” the bottlenecks - we do so.
    In other words, we partition Px,y into segments that are either a single α-distant edge, or
pairs of vertices with stretch ≤ α in H, and choose one whose segments cannot be merged
further; we call such segmentations minimal. Finally the (α, β)-completion is:
While there exist x, y such that:

    distH (x, y) > α · distG (x, y) + β.

Find an x-to-y shortest path Px,y . Compute a minimal segmentation of Px,y w.r.t H. Add
to H all the α-distant edges in the chosen segmentation.

       2.4      The (k, k − 1)-spanner algorithm, and its analysis

       initialization step is natural, and common in spanner constructions, see e.g. [20, 4, 19].

       several new adaptations. For simplicity we assume k is odd, and set R := k−1                 2 . Let ti be

            We now explain the interplay between the above analysis and the designed completion.
       The bound we get on distH (s, s′ ) after the set-off iteration follows since in each greedy step
       the bottlenecks are added, hence every contiguous union of segments has stretch ≤ k. Since
       s, s′ are not on Px,y but are still somewhat close, they inherit the small stretch from the
       attaching points, up to the additive slack mentioned.
            The distance improvement of many pairs (s, s′ ) is quite natural, and follows since the
       pair x, y chosen does not satisfy the stretch guarantee. A tricky part of the proof is to show

       additive case to the (α, β) set-up.
            Finally, showing that finalized pairs are not part of the Ω(ti ) improving pairs again follows

 3        The Algorithm
Throughout, let G = (V, E) be a weighted graph, and let H ⊆ G be a subgraph. We assume
that every edge of G is itself a shortest path between its endpoints; otherwise, such an edge
may be safely removed without affecting the result.

3.1       Shortest paths and segmentations
For vertices x, y ∈ V , let Px,y = (x = x0 , x1 , . . . , xt = y) denote a shortest x–y path in G.

such that for every segment satisfying ik − ik−1 ≥ 2,

▶ Definition 8 (minimal segmentation). An α-segmentation S is minimal if no block of one
or more consecutive segments of S can be merged into a single segment so as to produce

▶ Definition 9 (Distant edges of a segmentation). Given an α-segmentation S of Px,y , denote

3. Find a minimal segmentation S of Px,y (w.r.t. the current H, G).
4. Update H ← H ∪ Eα (S, H).

       Computing the (α, β)-completion

       The (α, β)-completion can be computed in polynomial time. By Lemma 10 the loop runs
       O(|V |2 ) iterations. For a fixed iteration it remains to show that a minimal segmentation can
       be found efficiently. This can be done as follows: Start with the trivial segmentation of Px,y ,
       and repeatedly merge a block of consecutive segments whenever their union has stretch at
       most α in H. When no further merge is possible, the resulting segmentation is minimal.

and let S be the minimal segmentation of Px,y used in the completion step.
    Let e1 , e2 , . . . , et denote the edges in Ek (S, H), ordered along Px,y from x to y. Each edge
ei = (ui , vi ) has endpoints whose stretch in H is greater than k, i.e., distH (ui , vi ) > k · w(ei ).

the path from x to xnew , and y to ynew has stretch ≤ k so if x, y was chosen by the greedy

of generality, that x ∈ e1 , and y ∈ et .

 5      Final Remarks and Open Problems
A main open question left from this work is whether unweighted (α, β)-spanners can be
extended to the weighted setup? There are many (α, β) for which (α, β)-spanners exist for
unweighted graphs, though almost all constructions do not generalize; e.g., it is open whether
the construction of [9], as well as the recent constructions of [11] which have o(k) = α = Ω(1)
can be extended to the weighted setting.

▶ Question 26. Is it the case that if there is an unweighted (α, β)-spanner for some (α, β),
then there is a weighted (α, β)-spanner with a similar size guarantee.

    Recall that the lightness of a spanner is the ratio of its total weight divided by the weight
of a minimum spanning tree. We ask:

▶ Question 27. For which (α, β) can we provide an (α, β)-spanner with relatively small
lightness?

     Finally we propose the following more structural direction:

Where did the k − 1 go?
The keen reader may have noticed that in Section 3.3 the fact that distH (x, y) > k ·
distG (x, y) + (k − 1)W was not used. It actually appears only in Observation 14, hence under
the assumption that (x, y) have a minimal segmentation with more than one missing edge
we can run the completion algorithm under the same size bound and give the guarantee
distH (x, y) ≤ kdistG (x, y) + Wmax (G). As explained in Remark 18 the choice of the constant
1 is arbitrary. In fact, one can achieve the following: For any ε > 0, and any weighted graph
G there exist a subgraph H of size O(n e 1+1/k /ε) such that for any x, y, and any shortest path
Px,y between them in G one has:
    ((k, k − 1)-local stretch) distH (x, y) ≤ k · distG (x, y) + (k − 1)Wmax (Px,y ), where Px,y is
    an x to y shortest path. Or,
    (stretch k and additive +εWmax (G)) Namely, distH (x, y) ≤ k · distG (x, y) + εWmax (G).

    The proof follows from the analysis in Section 4. Pick a minimal segmentation S of
Px,y , and distinguish paths according to |Ek (S, H)| . If |Ek (S, H)| = 0 the first alternative
above clearly holds. If |Ek (S, H)| = 1, then by Observation 14 we have distH (x, y) ≤
k · distG (x, y) + (k − 1)w(e) where e is the missing edge, hence the first guarantee holds.
Finally if |Ek (S, H)| ≥ 2, then we check if the second guarantee holds, and if so we do not do
anything, if not, we add Ek (S, H). By changing the definition of improved pairs, Definition 17
to have distance difference between H, H ′ bigger than 2ε W . All parts of the proof stay
exactly the same, except for the final proof of Theorem 13, which needs to be augmented as
every pair of centers can improve O(k 2 /ε) times, yielding an 1/ε larger spanner.

▶ Question 28. Can one provide a better structural guarantee than being just an (α, β)
spanner for weighted graph? E.g. is it possible to ensure that for every x, y and any shortest
path Px,y , can be segmented into O(β) edges from G and paths of stretch α plus a relatively
negligible error?

    It is plausible that resolving the question above can provide a path to allow comparison
for the guarantees of (α, β)-spanners, for different α’s and β’s, similarly to the unweighted
setup.
